The experiment focuses on three core areas: Situation Assessment: Environment perception based on camera images and robot state Task Planning: Multi-step planning and execution from natural-language instructions Robot Control: Feedback-driven object manipulation and mobile manipulation Here is the system architecture and execution flow: Model Inference and Tool Calling: Connected via the Codex App Server, GPT-6 Astra checks the current camera view and robot state, then calls functions that specify the absolute target position and orientation for the selected hand. Harness and ROS 2 Control: The harness validates the model’s tool calls and translates them into ROS 2 and control commands to drive the robot. Observation and Feedback Loop: Once a motion finishes, the harness collects updated camera images, robot state, and execution results to return to the model, which then determines the next action based on that feedback. In the documentation, we also organized the reproducible execution environment and the engineering insights gained during testing: Simulation and Real Hardware Support: You can run the exact same structure in both the Gazebo tabletop environment and on the physical AI Worker. Isolated Credential Path: We configured the environment variables so the harness references authentication credentials without conflicting with existing setups. Real-Time Monitoring: Through the video bridge and viewer, you can track live camera streams and per-episode execution logs directly in your browser. Safety Parameters and Tradeoff Analysis: We cover how to configure the maximum step distance, maximum action count, and time limits, and openly share the pros and cons observed during testing, including visual feedback recovery cases alongside limitations in 2D image depth estimation, collision conditions, repeatability, and response latency. Although current limitations exist in API latency and execution reliability, this experiment confirms the potential of Agentic AI × Physical AI by connecting AI reasoning directly to physical robot actions. items.title: [STVL] New Obstruction Zones!
items.summary: Howdy everyone - your friendly neighborhood navigator here! I wanted to let you know quickly about a new feature in STVL that I think is very useful for the community - Obstruction Zones ! Courtesy of Remco , these allow you to specify occlusions to your sensors to treat them specially in the decay functions so that they remain present when in-bounds of the sensor frustum so they aren’t actively decayed. STVL was originally designed with high-visibility sensor configurations in mind (8+ RGBD cameras; top mounted 3D lidar) so this is a wonderful addition for those with dead areas in the sensor FOV due to self-collision or similar. Pull request SteveMacenski/spatio_temporal_voxel_layer [ros2] added obstruction polygons to 3d lidar frustrum (#367) ros2 ← remco-r:feature/ros2_obstruction_polygons remco-r opened 08:22PM - 21 Oct 26 UTC +687 -12 ## Add FOV Obstruction Polygons for 3D Lidar Frustum I introduced the option … to add "obstruction polygons" to the 3D lidar frustum. This way obstructions which are part of the robot body are considered out of field of view and persist accordingly.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
items.articleText: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.summary: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.articleText: The October inflection point for vibe game development Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: WorkOS Airlock — intent-based access control for AI agents. Request early access The October inflection point for vibe game development 28th October 2026 I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did . In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance. I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. Tree Appreciator The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here’s the chat transcript that built it. It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. Emberwick This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here’s that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll Here’s that version . When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here’s that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”. Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well. Battle Drones This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”. I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely. It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off. Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you. It’s absurdly cute. You can play the latest version here . I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet—it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors. Here’s the initial brainstorming session , which resulted in this spec file . Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it. I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true. This isn’t my best game yet—it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones—but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal—something that wouldn’t have been built in the before-times. Four times as insulting If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once . I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself. The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve’s Steam Next Fest is a good recent example. We now have games where everything —code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself—can be outsourced to the models. And the results don’t suck! Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone! I expect that, as we’ve already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction! I certainly won’t be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions—I don’t feel like I’ve earned that right. We’ll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects. What happens if someone actually puts the work in? The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input . The projects I’ve described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I’ve put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself). items.articleText: Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model Oct 28, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates. Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem. We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible. Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price 1 as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price. Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena . State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative. Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails): Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark ExploitGym (54.8%). Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench , turning validated findings directly into working code fixes. Advancing frontier model safety & security Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our Safety and Security report . With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way. Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%. Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence. Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon. Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope. Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt. Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon. items.title: Oseberg Tapestry Fragments
items.articleText: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia Fragments of tapestry discovered in the Oseberg ship burial in Norway Oseberg Tapestry Fragments Year 834AD Medium Silk, Flax Location Viking Ship Museum in Oslo, Norway The Oseberg tapestry is a fragmentary tapestry, discovered within the Viking Oseberg ship burial in Norway . The tapestry (dated to about 834AD )[ 1] is 16 to 23 centimeters in width, but the full length is unknown. The tapestry is filled with a large assortment of human and animal figures with varying interpretations. It is made from wool, silk, and flax. The fragments were found in 1904 in Norway inside of a well-preserved Viking ship, along with numerous other grave goods and two female bodies. Discovery and excavation [ edit ] The Oseberg find was excavated in the summer of 1904 on the Oseberg farm at Slagen, not far from Tønsberg .[ 2] The burial mound was excavated by Professor Gabriel Gustafson and his team from the University of Oslo .[ 1] Due to the amount of clay , soil , and peat packed together so tightly, it allowed for an unbelievable quality of preservation of all the wooden objects and also all other organic materials contained in the ship, including the ship itself. It is thought to be the best-preserved grave from the Viking Age .[ 1] Unfortunately, the ship and all of the contents inside were not left undisturbed until its 1904 excavation. Presumably around the Middle Ages , robbers had broken into the grave through a hole in the bow of the ship and into the burial chamber of the ship.[ 2] The entirety of the ship itself was also in poor shape, as the large amount of stones contained within the ship had caused considerable sinkage, and in turn, caused the ship to be broken up into thousands of pieces which then had to be painstakingly put back together.[ 2] The tapestry was one of a number of textile remains found in the Oseberg ship in 1904. Other finds included rolled-up rugs, tapestries, and curtains. Most are embroidered with mythological and battle scenes. There was no representation of the ship's owner.[ 3] Most of the textiles that were found within the ship were found in the burial chamber. They had also been pressed together in hard "cakes" due to the clay and soil that filled the inside of the ship, which had also been a very difficult job to disintegrate. Some of these textiles were also stuck to large clumps of feathers, which originally were in the beds of the burial chamber.[ 2] Remains [ edit ] At the entrance of the ship that the robbers had created, the skeletal remains of two people were found lying on the beds of the burial chamber. These remains that were found within the burial mound were assumed to be female, even prior to analysis of the physical remains themselves. Gustafson was able to come to the conclusion that this was a grave for a pair of women due to the textile remnants they were found with, along with tools for making textiles.[ 4] [ 5] The women were assumed to be some kind of royalty due to the elaborate nature of the burial mound and its contents. They have been labeled as queens, queen-consorts, widowed queens, or kings mothers.[ 4] The skeletal remains of horses, oxen, and dogs were also found in and around the burial mound.[ 1] [ 5] Other grave goods [ edit ] Most of the artifacts that were buried within the ship alongside the women were found in the forepart of the ship.[ 5] Many of the ship’s tools such as the oars, a gangway, a bailing vessel, tubs, pails, etc. were found here. There was also an ornamented cart, decorated sleighs, and a wood sled found within these artifacts.[ 1] Skeletons of animals were also found in and around the ship.[ 5] [ 1] Some personal effects that were found with these women were chests, buckets, and carved posts in the shape of animal heads. There was no jewelry found on or around the remains, which led archaeologists to come to the conclusion that any had been stolen by the robbers, as personal jewelry is an important factor in a Viking woman’s burial.[ 5] Description [ edit ] The tapestry is in poor condition and is assumed to be a part of the funeral offering of the ship burial. Due to its state of decay several years were required for its extraction, and today its extraction is still yet to be completed.[ 2] The tapestries consist of an assortment of both people and animals, as well as ships, wagons, and houses. The tapestry is an example of both Viking Age narrative art , and decorated textiles from Scandinavia in this period, both of which being extremely rare survivors.[ 6] The two largest, which are also the most well-preserved fragments, depict figures of armed people and animals moving to the left as if they are part of a funeral procession or religious ceremony.[ 3] [ 6] The precession is headed towards a great tree with corpses hanging from it; it is unknown what this represents.[ 6] The fragments also contain a scene featuring two black birds hovering over a horse, possibly originally pulling a wagon as a part of the procession.[ 7] The most central and prominent figures in this scene are two covered, horse-drawn carriages.[ 3] Between them, there is an assortment of male and female figures walking and riding together, some carrying objects such as spears, which were seen as Odin 's special weapon.[ 3] [ 6] Some figures depicted in this procession appear to wear ritual costumes, as one figure is depicted in a horned helmet while another wears an animal-head mask.[ 6] Due to the loss of most of its original coloring, the material of these fragments consists mostly of shades of brown and grey.[ 3] Oseberg tapestry detail Interpretations [ edit ] It is unknown what these tapestries are supposed to represent despite their images and figures.[ 3] There have been many differentiating interpretations of the fragments, such as that this tapestry depicts an actual funeral procession or even the funeral ceremony in Oseberg itself.[ 3] Anne Stine Ingstad interprets these birds as Huginn and Muninn flying over a covered cart containing an image of Odin with a horned helmet, drawing comparison with the images of the goddess Nerthus who is attested by Tacitus in 1 A.D. [ 7] The tapestry is stylistically similar to the Bayeux Tapestry , because of its narrative art style, colors, and overall movement of the forms. The figures in the Oseberg tapestry move horizontally such as those in the Bayeux Tapestry. Both are also referred to as “tapestries” while they are both embroideries, since the design is not woven into the cloth.[ 8] [ 9] Materials [ edit ] The fragments are all made from wool and silk , as well as other plant-based materials such as flax , which have since disintegrated prior to their discovery.[ 2] There is no trace of linen in the tapestry due to the condition that it was found in, but flax was cultivated into linen during this time period, and tools used for linen work were also found within the ship. It is assumed that the silk was imported, while the woolen contents were native work.[ 2] Historical context [ edit ] Viking burials [ edit ] The living had a duty to care for the dead and bury them, and all of the dead were treated with the utmost respect, no matter who they were. The first step of the burial is typically the treatment of the body. Both the eyes and the mouth of the body were shut, and they were washed with their hair combed. Following the treatment, the body was then placed on a straw bed, and after a number of days the corpse could then either be buried or burnt.[ 10] Inhumation was the most common form of burial, typically in some kind of coffin, or in more elaborate cases, in a chamber. Cremation was also occasionally practiced.[ 11] Following the treatment of the body, if the body was intended to be buried, a grave would be formed. These graves could be created in a variety of forms such as, circular, triangular, oval, or in the shape of a boat.[ 10] Sometimes they were surrounded by stones. If the graves were flat, sometimes, such as in the case of the Oseberg burial, mounds were created.[ 10] The dead were typically buried with objects and utensils from their daily life. Some grave goods also served a symbolic function, such as boats and wagons, like in the Oseberg burial, were a representation of their journey into the afterlife.[ 11] These items were all intended to equip the dead for their journey into the next world.[ 10] They were also sometimes accompanied by their dogs or horses.[ 11] The dead in cremation graves could also be accompanied by grave goods.[ 11] Textiles [ edit ] Textiles from the Viking Age are very diverse, with a variety of different weave styles, along with colored patterning, dyeing, and decorative additions.[ 12] There was a need for this wide variety of styles. Textiles were needed for clothing, whether it was everyday garb or special costumes. They were needed for upholstery, bedding, carpets, and wall hangings, as well as many other purposes. One of the most important needs for textiles was for sails and tents.[ 13] The materials varied, primarily wool and plant fibers such as flax, but other materials like silk, gold, and silver threads were also used.[ 13] Textile fragments have been found in many different burials, along with textile tools.[ 13] The manufacture of textiles was important during the Viking Age, but it also required the work of several people. The production process included the harvesting of the fibers and then preparing them for spinning and weaving, before finally sewing them into the finished product.[ 13] Textiles and the raw material required for textile production were traded and exchanged for valuable goods.[ 13] References [ edit ] Wikimedia Commons has media related to Oseberg tapestry fragments . 1 2 3 4 5 6 Vedeler, Marianne (2014). ## Security: Node.js runtime and CA certificate updates (October 2026)

On October 20, 2026, eMudhra disclosed that the private keys for eight of its intermediate CA certificates could be recovered from the public certificates. On October 21, Node.js shipped [security releases](https://nodejs.org/en/blog/vulnerability/october-2026-security-releases) that update its bundled CA certificates for the compromise and fix several unrelated high-severity runtime CVEs. On October 23, Python's `certifi` 2026.10.23 removed the eMudhra roots `emSign Root CA - C1` and `emSign ECC Root CA - C3`.

**How these servers stand**

- **The TypeScript servers rely on the Node.js runtime for certificate checks.** They ship no CA certificates of their own. Only `server-everything` makes outbound HTTPS requests (`gzip-file-as-resource`), and the Node.js it runs on verifies them. `server-filesystem`, `server-memory` and `server-sequential-thinking` make no network connections.
- **`mcp-server-fetch` verifies HTTPS against the `certifi` bundle**, through `httpx`. Installing from PyPI (`uvx mcp-server-fetch`, `pip install mcp-server-fetch`) resolves the current `certifi`, 2026.10.23 or later. The repository's `fetch` Dockerfile installs from its lockfile, which this release moves to `certifi` 2026.10.23 (#5341).
- **`mcp-server-git` and `mcp-server-time` make no network connections.**

**If you run a TypeScript server from npm (`npx` or a global install)**

It runs on your Node.js, which we can't update for you. Please run Node.js **24.22.1 or 26.12.1, or later**, and check with `node --version`. The packages' `engines` field accepts any Node.js 24, so npm won't warn you about an older, unpatched runtime.

**If you run `mcp-server-fetch` from an existing environment**

An environment created before October 23 keeps its older `certifi`. Refresh it with `uvx --refresh mcp-server-fetch`, or `pip install -U certifi`.

items.title: North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3
items.summary: Robot demand from automotive component manufacturers nearly doubled in Q3, as other sectors posted strong gains, reported A3. The post North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3 appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: While automotive OEM orders declined in the first half of 2026, they picked up in Q3. Source: A3 North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the Association for Advancing Automation, or A3. Orders increased 24.8% in units and 26.1% in value compared with the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far, it said. The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, A3 reported. This represented increases of 9.6% in units and 13.3% in value over the same period last year , noted the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization . Orders grow in automotive in addition to other industries After declining during the first half of 2026, automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5%, said A3. Orders from automotive component suppliers climbed 90.4%, continuing the strong demand from that segment seen earlier in the year. Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3: Semiconductors and electronics /photonics: +97.6% units Plastics and rubber: +67.7% units Life sciences /pharmaceutical /biomedical : +38.7% units Metals: +37.0% units All other industries increased just 0.5% in units ordered, while food and consumer goods declined by 23.7%, A3 added. The growth in the electronics segment occurred as investment grew in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, with strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others, said A3. Automotive component orders were particularly strong despite earlier weakness among automotive manufacturing, said the organization. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17% below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026. “What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” stated Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3. “Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while automotive components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.” Submit your innovation now! Cobot orders increase 56%, finds A3 Force- and power-limited or collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered. This was an increase of about 56% in units compared with Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7% of all robot units ordered during the quarter. Through September, North American companies ordered 4,605 cobots valued at approximately $178 million, representing 15.9% of total robot units and 9.4% of order value. Collaborative robots continue to be used across a wide range of applications and industries. In the first nine months of 2026, cobots accounted for 43.8% of robot orders in life sciences/pharma/biomed and 36.9% in semi & electronics/photonics. Manufacturing activity continues expansion The stronger robot order numbers come alongside improving manufacturing activity, said A3. The September Institute of Supply Chain Management (ISM) Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 54.5, marking a ninth consecutive month of expansion, while the Federal Reserve said that U.S. manufacturing output increasing 0.3% in September. Higher input costs, trade uncertainty, and the timing of large manufacturing projects remain factors to watch, noted A3. “But with robot orders strengthening across several industries, the North American market enters the final quarter of 2026 with positive momentum,” it said. More detailed Q3 2026 market data and graphs are available upon request for press and through the A3 Vault for member companies. A3 said it is the leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. A3 has also expanded its Market Intelligence resources with “Business of Automation ,” a weekly show examining industry developments; Business of Automation on Substack , offering additional analysis and industry updates; and SIGNAL , a free research series covering robotics, automation, and AI. Association members seeking deeper insights can subscribe to MI+ for forecasts, detailed datasets, dashboards and industry analysis. A3 members represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, system integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms. Tell Us What You Think! items.title: What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers
items.summary: Symbotic’s growth with Walmart shows how an anchor customer can fund a robotics startup’s scale while creating risks around customer concentration, contractual restrictions and the challenge of building a diversified, repeatable business. The post What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Symbotic’s recent quarterly filing lists its largest customer, together with affiliates, as “Customer A,” and the annual report names that customer as Walmart. Customer A supplied 90.5% of revenue in the quarter that ended June 27, 2026. Symbotic reported $720.8 million in revenue and $55 million in net income for the same quarter. Few robotics companies have turned one demanding customer into a business this size, and this profit follows earlier profits . The quarter also included $19.4 million of investment gains and negative non-GAAP free cash flow, so one quarter’s profit can’t settle whether leaning so heavily on Walmart has paid off. For a startup founder deciding whether to sign a second customer soon, Walmart’s 90.5% share says little about the cost of serving another account. I’d look at how many people that account pulls into the field and what the contract obliges each side to do when plans change. I’d also ask how easily the anchor could get the same work done another way. Walmart wrote its own insurance Symbotic can’t afford to lose Walmart, and that dependence already gives the retailer some protection. Walmart’s contracts show that it didn’t rely on that incentive alone. The 2022 master automation agreement gives Walmart continuity rights, including the right to embed engineers with Symbotic and technical material held in escrow, which Walmart can use under specified conditions. The 2025 agreement for Walmart’s store-level Accelerated Pickup and Delivery (APD) systems repeats those protections. During the APD build-out, it also caps, at a redacted number, how many comparable APD systems Symbotic can sell to each outside customer every year. The filings don’t show whether Walmart has ever tested these rights, so they read more like preparation than a proven fallback. When the APD deal closed in January 2025, Walmart committed $520 million of development funding. Symbotic paid Walmart a $200 million base price for its robotics business in the same transaction and agreed to two possible milestone payments of $175 million each. Symbotic gained funded development and the prospect of a large rollout, although the additional purchase commitment depends on performance milestones. In return, it accepted delivery obligations and limits on comparable APD sales to other customers. Every new site borrows people Operations-heavy robotics companies tend to add people as they add customers, at least until deployment becomes routine. Symbotic reported about 2,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025, with roughly half working at customer sites to install, commission, and maintain its systems, and it brings in contractors as needed. Its standard model also has Symbotic operate a new system for a limited time before handing daily operation to the customer. Those field teams serve both new deployments and running systems, so the total can’t show what one more site would take. It does show how much of the business still happens where the robots are installed. Where the newer Symbotic demand comes from Symbotic has broadened its customer base, partly through structures it helped build. Exol, its warehouse-as-a-service venture with SoftBank, accounted for $11.6 billion of the $22.5 billion backlog at June 27, 2026, and Symbotic owns 35% of Exol and helps fund its build-out. Walmart de México, another newer customer, is majority-owned by Walmart. Exol lets customers use Symbotic’s system without buying it outright, and Walmex carries a proven relationship into a new market, so both routes make commercial sense. Both also move partly with decisions made by Symbotic or Walmart, so the longer customer list carries somewhat less independent demand than its length suggests. Submit your innovation now! A new Symbotic customer can take two years to go live Symbotic’s management said in 2023 that it aimed to add one or two new customers a year. It has also described its historical timeline as about 24 months from a signed statement of work to acceptance. Medline signed in late fiscal 2025 and plans a pilot in 2027. Associated Wholesale Grocers announced a project in March 2026 and expects operations in the fourth quarter of 2027. Associated Food Stores announced its agreement in May 2023 and had its first phase running by February 2025. Symbotic generally recognizes system revenue as it incurs costs, once acceptance is reasonably assured, so revenue can start before installation and well before go-live. The 24-month timeline instead shows how long a supplier can wait before a new customer’s site actually runs, which is when it learns whether the product traveled. What I expect and what would change my mind The scenario I would examine most closely has no villain. Walmart stays satisfied, meets its commitments, and finishes the distribution-center rollout on schedule. System revenue from that program then winds down, and the work that continues, mostly service and software, brings in less than installation did unless new system orders follow. The supplier did everything right, and its growth now depends on replacing a program that ended as planned. For Symbotic, the APD program and Exol are the obvious candidates to replace it, along with newer accounts, and I would watch whether they reach real scale before the distribution-center work tapers. I expect Walmart to remain Symbotic’s dominant customer for years, and I’d be surprised to see its share fall below 80% before fiscal 2028. Walmart keeps expanding its own commitments, with the performance-dependent APD program added on top of the distribution-center rollout. New accounts tend to start with one site or a pilot, and management’s stated aim in 2023 was one or two new customers a year. Even with revenue recognized as costs are incurred, a single new site adds little next to dozens of Walmart projects moving at once. Exol is my largest uncertainty. Its revenue counts outside Walmart, so a faster build-out of its contracted systems could pull down Walmart’s reported share, even though I would still treat Exol separately when judging independent demand. A faster Exol ramp, or larger near-term rollouts by unrelated customers, would change my view. I also expect strategic buyers to lean harder on contractual control. Protective terms of this kind already appear in automation contracts. I think buyers who invest in warehouse and humanoid startups, or deploy their robots at scale, will ask for them more often and in broader forms. The same field-load logic explains why I expect a shakeout among humanoid pilots over the next few years. A pilot at one site with a few robots can run on subsidy. The robot maker’s engineers can install the robots, step in when one stalls, and absorb support costs that the pilot price doesn’t recover. A fleet contract tends to turn those hidden costs into obligations. When the buyer pays a fixed service price for uptime, extra interventions come out of the vendor’s margin. The humanoid companies that reach paid fleets will probably be the ones that used their pilots to measure and cut the field work each robot needs. A famous customer or a large funding round won’t guarantee that step. If several of these companies grow paid fleets and keep support costs predictable, I’d expect a milder shakeout than I do now. What startups can take from Symbotic Walmart got continuity rights and limits on Symbotic’s comparable sales in exchange for funding and scale. I think founders tend to judge an anchor deal by the size of the order and skim terms like these. A better habit is to go through the contract clause by clause and ask what each restriction costs in buyers the company can no longer pursue. The money deserves the same scrutiny, since every dollar comes with something to deliver or repay. That funding goes furthest when it buys repeatability. Symbotic’s management has described moving testing to suppliers and standardizing build and test procedures, work that can pay off on every later deployment. Startups do the same fieldwork with far fewer people. A second customer on the same system still pulls staff into the field, and one that needs a different integration pulls more of them, usually off the anchor’s rollout. Because the same small team tends to carry both jobs, a new logo can slow the anchor when it is paying the bills. As an operator, I would track field hours and unplanned engineering time across comparable deployments, the measure Symbotic’s filings can’t give outsiders. When design engineers keep getting pulled in to solve problems already solved at earlier sites, the product is still in development. It’s ready to scale once the team can predict and price the engineering and field work each new site requires. Symbotic’s timeline is a reason to start testing with a second customer well before the anchor’s rollout slows. An early project with a defined scope and budget can show how much effort another account really takes. Rajat Bhageria of Chef Robotics has described combining multiple customers’ requirements into one product specification and charging modest non-recurring engineering fees before building. That way, several buyers shape one product without a one-off project for each. Adding accounts for revenue is a different decision, because it commits people. It belongs after the team can estimate what a new site takes and deliver it alongside existing projects. Exol and Walmex also change how I would size a customer base. A buyer owned or funded by an existing partner tends to move with that partner, so independent budgets tell me more than the number of logos. AutoStore reached about 1,300 end customers through 23 distribution partners in fiscal 2025, yet four partners supplied 74% of its revenue. Concentration tends to move more easily than it disappears, so the real choice is which kind the company can survive. Before hiring ahead of anchor demand, it pays to model two scenarios. One is a six-month pause in the rollout. The other is the rollout finishing on schedule, the no-villain case above, which tends to get left out of plans because it looks like success. A Bossa Nova mobile shelf-scanning robot at work in a Walmart store. Source: Bossa Nova Robotics What not to copy The lesson I would leave behind is the concentration itself. Symbotic’s founder, Rick Cohen, also chairs C&S Wholesale Grocers, which gave Symbotic access to production environments during development, and Walmart later funded development directly. A startup whose anchor offers neither kind of support is making a different bet with the same percentage. I’d also look at the financial strength of both the robotics company and the business supporting it. In agricultural robotics, Root AI became part of a grower when AppHarvest bought it in 2021 . AppHarvest and its robotics subsidiary entered Chapter 11 in 2023, and the group’s court declaration pointed to farming losses and financing pressure. Zordi’s chief executive later announced that the company had bought AppHarvest’s robotics IP and assets, but the record doesn’t show whether Root AI could have stood on its own. Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021 , a year in which its apple-growing partner, T&G Global, stayed profitable, and its chief executive said the company couldn’t raise enough investment to finish development. Root AI went down with its parent company, and Abundant ran out of investors before it could finish its harvester. Walmart was also the main customer for Bossa Nova Robotics, a Carnegie Mellon spinout. By November 2020, Walmart had ended its relationship with the company, whose shelf-scanning robots had reached about 500 stores. Earlier that year, the companies had announced plans to reach 1,000 stores. The Wall Street Journal reported that employees picking online orders were giving Walmart another way to monitor inventory. items.title: Warp Sciences emerges from stealth, to apply robotics to drug research
items.summary: Warp Sciences has co-founders from OpenAI, Meta, and more, plus funding to build infrastructure for automated drug discovery in the U.S. The post Warp Sciences emerges from stealth, to apply robotics to drug research appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Warp Sciences plans to create chemistry infrastructure for sovereign biotech. Source: deni AI, Adobe Stock Warp Sciences last week emerged from stealth with $215 million in funding to create infrastructure that enables biotech and pharmaceutical companies to discover new medicines faster. The startup said it is building a U.S.-based chemistry contract research organization, or CRO, to bring together chemists, robotics, and AI to make and test molecules for research teams. The South San Francisco-based company ‘s stated goal is to provide experimental data to train better AI that in turn enables more capable labs, giving scientists the ability to test more ideas. “AI has dramatically accelerated software engineering and mathematics, but it has yet to make the same impact in the physical sciences,” stated Kevin Weil , co-founder and CEO of Warp Sciences. “Chemistry and biology move forward when you make something, test it and learn from the result.” “If we want to build more capable AI for science, we need to generate real-world data at scale,” he added. “Warp is starting that process by making the research compounds drug discovery needs today, while building the labs and automation to speed the cycle from hypothesis to experiment to answer.” Warp said it has no proprietary drug pipeline itself; it is designing automated labs that can run experiments, learn from them, and improve with each cycle. Warp Sciences focuses on sovereign biotechnology A promising molecular design is only the beginning, observed Warp Sciences. “Scientists have to make it, test it, and use what they learn to decide what comes next,” said the company. “Faster access to compounds gives research teams faster answers, more ideas to pursue, and more opportunities to find medicines that change lives.” Warp also noted the importance of sovereign biotechnology. In a 2024 survey by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, 74% reported contracts with Chinese companies for preclinical and clinical services, according to Reuters. The BIOSECURE Act , signed into law in December 2025, established a framework for restrictions on federal procurement and funding involving designated biotechnology companies of concern. In response, Warp claimed that it is building a U.S.-based chemistry partner that scientists can rely on for its speed, quality, and close collaboration. Its goal is to shorten the path from molecular design to testing while giving customers more control over where sensitive research takes place. The company said its initial service will focus on lead optimization analog synthesis, making variations of molecules that scientists can compare as they search for a drug candidate. Experienced chemists will guide experiments as the lab is increasingly automated by robotics and AI, with AI models trained on data from physical experiments. Warp plans to enable its customers to discover drugs more efficiently and keep that discovery in the U.S. Submit your innovation now! Founders’ expertise spans AI and healthcare Warp Sciences noted that its founding team ’s experience spans AI, data infrastructure, healthcare, and drug discovery. Weil most recently served as chief product officer and vice president of science at OpenAI . Chief Scientific Officer Solomon “Sol” Reisberg held medicinal chemistry leadership roles at Terremoto Biosciences. “I’ve worked with overseas chemistry partners that delivered speed and value, but I still worried about protecting the intellectual property behind our programs,” said Reisberg. “We’re building Warp to give drug hunters that same caliber of chemistry services in the U.S., with IP protection at the center of the relationship, and without the price premium that U.S. boutique CROs currently demand.” Chief Technology Officer “Manohar “Mano” Paluri was a vice president at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a founding member of FAIR. DJ Patil was a founding executive at Devoted Health and the first U.S. chief data scientist for the White House. “Our goal is simple: Every experiment should make the next one smarter,” Paluri asserted. “AI needs a closer connection to the physical work of chemistry. Closing the loop between designing experiments, executing them, and learning from their outcomes builds increasingly capable systems for deciding what to make and how to make it. We’re building the software, AI and robotics alongside the lab so each part is shaped by what chemists actually need.” Early hires have added robotics experience from companies including Genesis , Skild AI , and 1X Technologies , as well as scientific expertise from Genentech and Lawrence Livermore National Labs. “Warp’s services bolster customer-led discovery programs. Our biotech and pharma customers determine which molecules to pursue and retain control of their drug programs,” said Patil. “We’re not developing drugs of our own. We’re building the infrastructure for the people who do.” Venture capital firms, angel investors support Warp Lightspeed led Warp Sciences’ funding, with participation from Premji Invest, Mayfield, IVP, Lux, Conviction, Menlo Ventures, 01 Advisors, Standard, Lowercarbon Capital, Gigascale Capital, Angular Ventures, Scribble Ventures, Uncork Capital, Innovation Endeavors, Matter VP, Zero Shot Fund, SignalFire and Moxxie Ventures. Angel investors included Brian Armstrong (Coinbase CEO), Mike Krieger (Anthropic Labs co-lead, Instagram co-founder), Milan Kovac (former Tesla Robotics vice president), and Ion Stoica (Databricks co-founder). It also included Fidji Simo (former OpenAI AGI Deployment CEO), Brendan Foody (Mercor CEO), Mark Chen (OpenAI chief research officer), and Sarah Friar (OpenAI chief financial officer). In addition, Kate Rouch (former OpenAI and Coinbase chief marketing officer), Lulu Meservey (Rostra CEO), Deepak Pathak (Skild AI CEO), Dylan Field (Figma CEO), and Lachy Groom (Physical Intelligence co-founder and chief operating officer) were angel investors. items.articleText: NVIDIA RTX Spark powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do. RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere. New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark. The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support. Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents. Phantom Blade Zero , S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5. Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark. Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe Introduced today, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages. Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to: “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.” “Translate this audio into English.” “List what decisions were made in this meeting.” Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the Hugging Face Open ASR and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware. It’s available today on Hugging Face . Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM. Learn more in the NVIDIA technical blog . Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment. With the new resource management feature in NVIDIA App , users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster. Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings. Liquid AI : One Model Family, Many Ways to Work Liquid AI’s LFM3 provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model. These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests. Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally. ‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5 S-GAME’s Phantom Blade Zero launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on Steam and the Epic Games Store . Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy. NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate. Read more on GeForce.com . RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics NVIDIA RTX Remix , the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft . Both creators and players can render Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations. The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to Portal with RTX and the Half-Life 2 RTX demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up path tracing. RTX Remix 1.6 also makes AI-powered modding simpler. A redesigned ComfyUI workflow lets modders generate physically based materials directly inside RTX Remix, with no application programming interface setup, batch processing for full projects and presets for less technical creators. Plus, with NVIDIA agent skills, compatible AI agents can work directly with RTX Remix to help speed up remastering projects. Learn more in the RTX Remix blog . RTX Spark Laptops: Beautifully Designed, Built for Everything RTX Spark laptops come in a range of designs, so users can choose one that fits how they work and play. Options include different screen sizes, colors, touchscreens, pen support and two-in-one convertibles. RTX Spark laptops are as thin as 14mm and as light as three pounds, with all-day battery life. Such slim designs are possible because RTX Spark places the GPU, CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory on one power-efficient superchip. Creative projects and AI models draw from the same memory pool, so a laptop can take on work that used to call for a desktop workstation, even when unplugged. Here’s what this means for: AI developers: Run models and agents locally on NVIDIA CUDA — the same platform that powers AI in the cloud — with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. Creators: RTX Spark can edit camera native 4:2:2 video and render 3D scenes of up to 90GB. Adobe Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases. Gamers: Hundreds of games run on RTX Spark, with NVIDIA DLSS, ray tracing, Reflex and G-SYNC delivering sharper visuals and smoother, more responsive gameplay. RTX Spark laptops are available now from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, starting at $2,599, with 128GB configurations on shelves. Find a laptop on the RTX Spark product page . #ICYMI: More Updates From NVIDIA Local AI 🦆Microducks learn to walk with help from RTX Spark: During the GTC Berlin keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed how AI agents running on RTX Spark can help train Hugging Face’s Microduck robot . A new NVIDIA technical blog walks through the workflow: Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt plan an obstacle course on RTX Spark, Astra builds the 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Lab trains the navigation policy and RTX Spark validates it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Watch the demo and try the playbook . ⚡ NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB is now available , enabling natural conversations and multistep agent tasks with as little as 4GB of memory. The model powers local voice assistants, game characters and embedded interfaces on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, GeForce RTX GPUs and NVIDIA Jetson devices. It supports llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio, and works with Hermes and OpenClaw. For more demanding agent workloads, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is designed to run local agents on RTX Spark. 🖼️Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights model that lets users generate and edit images locally. NVIDIA-optimized versions run on RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM. Developers can also fine-tune the model on RTX Spark using an NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel recipe to customize it for specific creative workflows. 🖥️ NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners, giving developers and researchers another way to build and run AI locally. Powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, it combines 64GB of unified memory with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack for agent development, inference and fine-tuning. Learn more and explore purchase options . Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X , Instagram , TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter . Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X . See notice regarding software product information. report.one_sentence_summary: GPT-6 Astra 기반 로봇 제어와 STVL 차폐 보존 기능이 공개되고, Gemini 4 Carbon 및 Nemotron 3.5 출시와 함께 북미 로봇 주문 증가와 바이오 로보틱스 투자가 확인되었습니다.
report.section_robotics:
- **GPT-6 Astra 및 Codex 기반 로봇 제어 환경**: Codex를 통해 GPT-6 Astra와 AI Worker를 연결하여 사전 정책 학습 없이 비전과 로봇 상태를 바탕으로 제어 도구를 호출하고 검증하는 실험 환경을 마련했으며, Gazebo 시뮬레이션과 실물 AI Worker 로봇 하드웨어 모두에서 동일한 제어 구조를 재현할 수 있습니다 [2].
- **STVL Obstruction Zones**: 센서 절두체 내 특정 차폐 영역을 별도 처리하여 로봇 본체 등으로 가려진 사각지대 장애물이 감쇠 함수로 인해 삭제되지 않고 유지되도록 지원합니다 [3].
- **GTK4 기반 ROS 2 GUI Installer**: RUNTIME Robotics가 초보자의 설치 편의를 위해 오픈소스로 공개한 도구로, Workshop Profiles 기능을 통해 YAML 파일로 패키지 구성 및 설치 환경을 복제해 워크숍 참가자에게 공유할 수 있습니다 [4].
report.section_devtools:
- **Google DeepMind Gemini 4 Carbon**: SEC-bench Pro 88.2%, ExploitGym 54.8%, CWE-bench 71.0%를 기록하며 보안 취약점 탐지 및 패치 성능을 개선했고, 초기 가격은 100만 입력 토큰당 2달러, 출력 토큰당 10달러로 책정되었습니다 [9, 14].
- **MCP Servers v2.2.0**: eMudhra 중간 CA 인증서 개인키 노출 이슈에 대응해 Node.js 런타임 보안 업데이트 권고와 certifi 2026.10.23을 반영하고, server-filesystem 2.1.0 등 패키지의 버그 수정 및 파일 경로 처리를 개선했습니다 [16].
- **NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 및 GPU 리소스 제어**: 전사, 화자 구분, 번역을 단일 모델로 처리하는 약 43억 활성 파라미터의 오픈 웨이트 음성 모델을 Hugging Face에 공개하고, NVIDIA App을 통해 포그라운드 앱과 백그라운드 AI 에이전트 간 GPU 자원 분배 기능을 제공합니다 [21].
report.section_industry:
- **OpenAI·ServiceNow 파트너십 확장**: ServiceNow 플랫폼에 OpenAI 모델과 에이전트를 도입하고 ChatGPT 및 Codex에 ServiceNow 기업 워크플로를 연동하기 위해 협력을 확대했습니다 [6].
- **A3 2026년 3분기 북미 로봇 주문**: 북미 기업들의 로봇 주문이 총 10,989대(7억 2,350만 달러)로 전년 동기 대비 유닛 기준 24.8% 증가했으며, 협동 로봇(Cobot) 주문도 약 56% 늘어난 1,831대를 기록했습니다 [18].
- **Warp Sciences 신약 개발 인프라 투자 유치**: 화학자, 로보틱스, AI를 결합한 신약 합성 및 테스트 인프라 구축을 위해 2억 1,500만 달러 규모의 투자를 유치하며 스텔스 상태를 해제했습니다 [20].

draft.one_sentence_summary: GPT-6 Astra 기반 로봇 제어와 STVL 차폐 보존 기능이 공개되고, Gemini 4 Carbon 및 Nemotron 3.5 출시와 함께 북미 로봇 주문 증가와 바이오 로보틱스 투자가 확인되었습니다.
draft.section_robotics:
- **GPT-6 Astra 및 Codex 기반 로봇 제어 환경**: Codex를 통해 GPT-6 Astra와 AI Worker를 연결하여 사전 정책 학습 없이 비전과 로봇 상태를 바탕으로 제어 도구를 호출하고 검증하는 실험 환경을 마련했으며, Gazebo 시뮬레이션과 실물 AI Worker 로봇 하드웨어 모두에서 동일한 제어 구조를 재현할 수 있습니다 [2].
- **STVL Obstruction Zones**: 센서 절두체 내 특정 차폐 영역을 별도 처리하여 로봇 본체 등으로 가려진 사각지대 장애물이 감쇠 함수로 인해 삭제되지 않고 유지되도록 지원합니다 [3].
- **GTK4 기반 ROS 2 GUI Installer**: RUNTIME Robotics가 초보자의 설치 편의를 위해 오픈소스로 공개한 도구로, Workshop Profiles 기능을 통해 YAML 파일로 패키지 구성 및 설치 환경을 복제해 워크숍 참가자에게 공유할 수 있습니다 [4].
draft.section_devtools:
- **Google DeepMind Gemini 4 Carbon**: SEC-bench Pro 88.2%, ExploitGym 54.8%, CWE-bench 71.0%를 기록하며 보안 취약점 탐지 및 패치 성능을 개선했고, 초기 가격은 100만 입력 토큰당 2달러, 출력 토큰당 10달러로 책정되었습니다 [9, 14].
- **MCP Servers v2.2.0**: eMudhra 중간 CA 인증서 개인키 노출 이슈에 대응해 Node.js 런타임 보안 업데이트 권고와 certifi 2026.10.23을 반영하고, server-filesystem 2.1.0 등 패키지의 버그 수정 및 파일 경로 처리를 개선했습니다 [16].
- **NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe 및 GPU 리소스 제어**: 전사, 화자 구분, 번역을 단일 모델로 처리하는 약 43억 활성 파라미터의 오픈 웨이트 음성 모델을 Hugging Face에 공개하고, NVIDIA App을 통해 포그라운드 앱과 백그라운드 AI 에이전트 간 GPU 자원 분배 기능을 제공합니다 [21].
draft.section_industry:
- **OpenAI·ServiceNow 파트너십 확장**: ServiceNow 플랫폼에 OpenAI 모델과 에이전트를 도입하고 ChatGPT 및 Codex에 ServiceNow 기업 워크플로를 연동하기 위해 협력을 확대했습니다 [6].
- **A3 2026년 3분기 북미 로봇 주문**: 북미 기업들의 로봇 주문이 총 10,989대(7억 2,350만 달러)로 전년 동기 대비 유닛 기준 24.8% 증가했으며, 협동 로봇(Cobot) 주문도 약 56% 늘어난 1,831대를 기록했습니다 [18].
- **Warp Sciences 신약 개발 인프라 투자 유치**: 화학자, 로보틱스, AI를 결합한 신약 합성 및 테스트 인프라 구축을 위해 2억 1,500만 달러 규모의 투자를 유치하며 스텔스 상태를 해제했습니다 [20].

findings: 선정된 모든 항목이 원문 근거에 정확히 부합하며, 비기술적 잡담이나 단순 채용/삭제된 스레드가 적절히 배제되었음을 확인했습니다.
상대적 시점 표현('오늘', '이번 주')을 배제하고 수치 및 벤치마크 점수(SEC-bench Pro 88.2%, 10,989대 등)의 보존 상태를 검증했습니다.
기업 주장 및 커뮤니티 실험 결과를 객관적인 어조로 한정하여 기술했습니다.

Real-Time Monitoring: Through the video bridge and viewer, you can track live camera streams and per-episode execution logs directly in your browser.
